# The Da Hong Pao Mother Trees: The World’s Most Expensive Tea
By Shan ZhouJun 13, 2026[Da Hong Pao](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/da-hong-pao/)1,299 viewsUpdated Sep 20, 2026
![](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/the-da-hong-pao-mother-trees-cover-1024x576.jpg)
[Da Hong Pao](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/da-hong-pao/)
Six tea bushes grow on a cliff in the Wuyi Mountains, and in 2003 the local government insured them for 100 million yuan. They’re the Da Hong Pao [mother trees](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/chinese-tea-glossary/#mother-tree-da-hong-pao), the original plants the whole famous tea traces back to, and they’re often called the most expensive tea in the world. Twenty grams once sold at auction for more than the price of a car.
There’s a twist most people miss, though. No one has picked these trees since 2006, and the Da Hong Pao you can buy today doesn’t come from them at all. I’ve stood in the gorge at Jiulongke and looked up at them, and the real story is stranger and better than any price tag.
It comes down to one surprising choice the people of Wuyi made about their most valuable tea.
![Da Hong Pao mother trees key facts: six bushes, over 350 years old, Jiulongke cliff, insured for 100 million yuan, picking banned since 2006](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/da-hong-pao-mother-trees-facts-1024x768.png)

## Six Bushes on a Cliff
The Da Hong Pao mother trees aren’t what you picture. There’s no towering, dramatic “king of tea.” They’re a handful of ordinary-looking shrubs, thick-leaved and a little scraggly, clinging to a ledge partway up a steep red rock face in a narrow gorge called Jiulongke. Walk past without a guide and you might not give them a second look.
There are six of them today, and the count has a history. The earliest records mention three, once tended by the monks of the Tianxin temple. A fourth somehow appeared on the cliff ledge later, and in 1980, when a garden of famous Wuyi bushes was laid out, two more were planted.
That makes six. They’re roughly 350 years old, which isn’t ancient for a plant, but for a tea bush that’s been watched, recorded, and harvested by name for centuries, it’s remarkable.
![The Da Hong Pao mother trees growing on a steep rock face at Jiulongke in the Wuyi Mountains](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/da-hong-pao-mother-trees-cliff-1024x702.jpg)
They’ve been guarded for a long time. In the 1930s the local government posted soldiers to watch them, and after 1949 farmers were hired to keep an eye on them year-round. Today they sit inside the protected scenic area, watched around the clock, and only specialists get close.
When Wuyi was named a World Heritage site in 2000, the trees were added to China’s register of famous old trees. They grow on a thin skin of weathered grit, roots forced deep into the rock cracks for water and minerals, which is exactly the hard [Wuyi terroir](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/where-da-hong-pao-comes-from/) that gives this tea its character.
## The World’s Most Expensive Tea?
The numbers are genuinely hard to believe. The six trees together yield well under a kilogram of finished tea a year, when they were still picked at all, so each harvest was measured in grams. In 1998, at the first Wuyi Da Hong Pao festival, 20 grams of mother-tree tea sold at auction for 156,800 yuan. In 2005, another 20 grams went for 208,000 yuan.
Do the math and it lands somewhere absurd. That 2005 price works out to roughly 10,000 yuan a gram, which made the tea worth about ten times its weight in gold at the time. A normal pinch of leaf for one pot is seven or eight grams.
At those rates, brewing a single pot of it would pour away a few months of an ordinary salary. Then there’s the insurance: in 2003 the trees were covered for 100 million yuan, the kind of sum that buys a floor of an office tower.
![Da Hong Pao mother-tree auction prices: 20 grams sold for 156,800 yuan in 1998 and 208,000 yuan in 2005, with 100 million yuan insurance in 2003](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/da-hong-pao-auction-prices-1024x691.png)
It’s worth being honest about what those prices measure. You aren’t paying for a cup that tastes ten times better than a fine ordinary Da Hong Pao. You’re paying for rarity, for history, and for a moving piece of local pride. The flavor is real and it’s excellent, built on the rocky [yan yun](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/what-does-da-hong-pao-taste-like/) these cliffs produce.
But the price tag is mostly story. As I always say, at the top of any market, you stop paying for the tea and start paying for the legend around it. The same tea also has a famous diplomatic chapter, which I tell in full in the piece on the [name and legend](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/da-hong-pao-name-legend/).
## Why No One Picks Them Anymore
You’d expect tea this valuable to be picked down to the last leaf. The opposite happened. In 2006 the Wuyi authorities made an unusual call: they stopped harvesting the mother trees for good. The reasoning was simple and a little moving. The trees were old, there were only six, and squeezing a few more grams out of them each year was neither worth it nor dignified.
![The narrow Jiulongke gorge in the Wuyi Mountains, home of the Da Hong Pao mother trees](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/jiulongke-gorge-wuyi.jpg)
The last harvest came in May 2005. In 2007, the final 20 grams picked from the mother trees was formally handed to the National Museum of China to be kept. Think about what that gesture says. A thing that had always been a tea, something to drink, was reclassified as something to protect.
The moment a commodity becomes a museum piece, its whole identity changes. You can no longer drink it, only look at it, the way you’d look at any other national treasure behind glass.
That decision is the part of this story I find most worth telling. We live in an age that prizes cashing in: if you have a resource, use it; if you have value, realize it. Holding something back almost needs an excuse.
Yet the people who looked after these trees did the rare thing and chose not to use the most valuable tea they had. Expensive was never the highest honor here. Being protected, on purpose, was.

## So What Are You Actually Buying?
This is where most newcomers get fooled, so let’s be plain about it. The mother-tree leaf hasn’t entered the market for years. If a seller swears the tea in your cup came from those six bushes, they’re spinning you a fantasy. Forget the mother-tree story and buy by the cup and by a seller you trust instead.
What you can actually buy falls into two honest categories. One is tea grown from cuttings of the mother-tree cultivars, mainly [Qidan](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/chinese-tea-glossary/#qi-dan) and Beidou, propagated and planted across the Wuyi area. Because these are clones, there’s no “second generation” or “third generation”; they carry the same genes as the parent.
The other, and by far the most common, is a blend of several Wuyi rock teas built to a balanced, repeatable Da Hong Pao style.
![A row of small cups of Da Hong Pao laid out for tasting](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/da-hong-pao-tasting-cups-1024x588.jpg)
Neither of those is fake, and neither is something to look down on. A good clone from a real Wuyi hillside can be wonderful, and skilled blending is a genuine craft, not a cheat. The thing to keep straight is simpler. The name passes down, but the exact bushes, their age, and the fate the centuries pressed into them do not.
A gift-shop magnet of a famous painting is still not the painting. For the full breakdown of clone versus blend, and how to [tell what Da Hong Pao really is](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/what-is-da-hong-pao/), start with the basics guide.
## The Mother Trees Aren’t Even One Variety
Here the story takes one last strange turn. The six mother trees aren’t even a single variety. Genetic testing has shown all six differ from one another, and they’re usually sorted into three cultivars: Qidan, Beidou, and Queshe. Their leaves and budding times don’t match. “The mother trees” are really a small, mixed family rather than one pure mother plant.
There’s a reason for that. In the hard years of the last century, gardens were abandoned and the bushes were left to pollinate on their own, with bees carrying pollen from whatever tea grew nearby. Over generations the bloodlines blurred. So what the single, original Da Hong Pao bush actually was, before all that mixing, is something nobody can say for certain anymore.
That should make the whole thing feel like a letdown, and somehow it doesn’t. The mother trees were never really about a perfect, pure pedigree. They’re a record of a place and a craft: a cliff, a soil, a way of roasting, and a few centuries of people deciding this tea was worth watching over.
That’s the part that travels into every honest cup of [Wuyi rock tea](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/chinese-tea-glossary/#wuyi-rock-tea), clone or blend.
## What the Mother Trees Are Really Worth
So skip the auction records and the “I drank mother-tree Da Hong Pao” bragging. The trees’ real value isn’t a number. It’s the lesson sitting underneath all those headlines: when something becomes truly rare, the wisest move often isn’t to sell it harder, it’s to stop and protect it. Wuyi did exactly that.
For you as a drinker, the takeaway is freeing. You don’t need the mythical leaf to taste what makes this tea great. A well-made clone or a thoughtful blend from a good rocky hillside will show you the real rock-bone-and-flower character, for the price of a nice dinner rather than a car.
I’ve cupped plenty that deliver exactly that, and not one of them needed a legend to be worth drinking. Drink that, and you’ve understood Da Hong Pao better than anyone chasing a ghost from the cliff.
When you want to see how the famous trees fit into the wider picture, from the legend to the flavor to the buying, our [complete Da Hong Pao guide](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/da-hong-pao/) ties it together. ## Hi! I am Shan Zhou
![zigzag separator](https://www.chineseteaguide.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/zigzag-separator-1.svg)
I’m Shan Zhou, a Chinese tea appraiser and tea-mountain chronicler. For more than twenty years, I’ve judged Chinese tea the only way I trust: by where it grows, how it’s made, and how it actually tastes in the cup. I started in local markets buying green tea, then followed the leaf back to the gardens, the mountains, and the rooms where tea is made. Chinese Tea Guide is where I turn that first-hand experience into plain-English guides. The goal is simple: help you understand what’s really in your cup, spend less on the box and the story, and find the tea that actually suits you.
